The '''athel tamarisk'''<ref name=PLANTS-Tamarix/> (''Tamarix aphylla''), also known as the '''athel tree''' or simply '''athel''' ({{langx|ar|أثل}}, {{transliteration|ar|ʔaṯl}}), is the largest known species of ''[[Tamarix]]'', with heights up to {{convert|18|m|ft}}. It is an evergreen flowering tree, native across North, East, and Central Africa, through the Middle East, and into parts of Western and Southern Asia.

== Distribution ==
''Tamarix aphylla'' is found along watercourses in arid areas. It is very resistant to saline and alkaline soils.<ref name=fs-fed-tamaph/> Its range extends from latitude 35°N to 0°N, and its W–E range extends from [[Morocco]] and [[Algeria]] in [[North Africa]], eastwards to [[Egypt]], and south to the [[Horn of Africa]] and into Kenya. It is found in the [[Middle East]] and the [[Arabian Peninsula]], east through [[Iran]], and into [[Pakistan]], [[Afghanistan]], and [[India]].<ref name=CAB-2000/>

== Description ==
''Tamarix aphylla'' grows as a tree to {{convert|18|m|ft}} high. The tiny leaves are alternately arranged along the branches, and exude salt, which can form a crusted layer on the surface, and drop onto the ground beneath.<ref name=CAB-2000/> The species can reproduce by seed, by suckering, or from a cutting. It blooms from July till November.<ref name=Israel>{{cite web |title=Plants of the Bible {{!}} Tamarix aphylla |url=http://www.flowersinisrael.com/Tamarixaphylla_page.htm |website=www.flowersinisrael.com |access-date=22 May 2022}}</ref>

==Salt tolerance and collecting humidity==
The tree is known to be very tolerant of salts. It has been found that it excretes concentrated salty water from glands on its leaf surfaces; the water evaporates leaving a crust of crystals containing more than ten salts. Most of the crystals fall off, but the crystals of at least one, [[lithium sulphate]], remain stuck on the leaves. These particular crystals swell with the small amount of humidity in the atmosphere at night, and the leaves absorb the moisture, helped by an adhesive surface that holds on to the water.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Al-Handawi | first1=Marieh B. | last2=Commins | first2=Patrick | last3=Dinnebier | first3=Robert E. | last4=Abdellatief | first4=Mahmoud | last5=Li | first5=Liang | last6=Naumov | first6=Panče | title=Harvesting of aerial humidity with natural hygroscopic salt excretions | journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences | volume=120 | issue=45 | date=2023-11-07 | article-number=e2313134120 | issn=0027-8424 | pmid=37903263 | pmc=10636306 | doi=10.1073/pnas.2313134120 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite news| last=Simons | first=Paul | title=How desert shrub's salty 'sweat' collects water from dry air | newspaper=The Guardian | date=20 December 2023 | url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2023/dec/20/desert-shrub-sweat-water-dry-air-athel-tamarisk }}</ref>

== Uses ==
''Tamarix aphylla'' has been used as a windbreak and shade tree in agriculture and [[horticulture]] for decades, especially in dryer regions such as the western United States and central and western Australia. Due to its higher fire adaptability, it can be used as a barrier to fire. Even when dry, the wood of ''Tamarix'' is difficult to burn, due to the high ash content (30–40%) and higher salt content of its foliage. After a fire it usually regrows, unless the root-crown is destroyed.<ref name=fs-fed-tamaph/>

The nectar from the blossoms of ''Tamarix aphylla'' produces high-quality honey with a unique taste. Due to the drought- and salt-tolerant properties of the tree, it could be planted as an agroforestry species, as well as for reclamation of marginal lands. A vegetative propagation method for the tree using the [[aeroponics]] technique has recently been developed.<ref name=Sharma-Kataria-Shekhawat-2017/>

The wood of the tree is usable in several applications, having medium mechanical properties.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Mantanis | first1=George | last2=Bırbılıs | first2=Dimitrios | author1-link=George Mantanis  | title=PHYSICAL AND MECHANICAL PROPERTIES OF ATHEL WOOD (Tamarix aphylla) | journal=Turkish Journal of Forestry | publisher=Isparta University of Applied Sciences | volume=11 | issue=2 | date=2010-08-11 | issn=2149-3898 | doi=10.18182/tjf.29019 | pages=82–87 | doi-broken-date=1 July 2025 | url=https://dergipark.org.tr/en/pub/tjf/issue/20895/224369 | access-date=2024-11-21}}</ref>

=== Australia ===
Within these regions, it has spread, most dramatically and noticeably in central [[Australia]] after the floods of 1974 along the [[Finke River]] in the [[Northern Territory, Australia|Northern Territory]]. Since then it has become a serious weed and [[invasive species]] in the Northern Territory and Western Australia. The species had been present for many decades without much spread before this.<ref name=Griffin-Smith-etal-1989/>

It tends to use more water than most [[native plant]]s in Australia, which it outcompetes. It has replaced the indigenous [[eucalyptus]] along watercourses in the interior.<ref name=Griffin-Smith-etal-1989/> It has been declared [[Weeds of National Significance|a weed of national significance]] in Australia.<ref name=Weeds-Aus-athelpine/>

=== United States ===
It is commonly used for [[windbreak]]s on the edges of [[Field (agriculture)|agricultural fields]] and as a [[shade tree]] in the [[desert]]s of the Southwestern [[United States]]. This species has not naturalized in areas of the United States where it has been grown, unlike other species in the genus ''[[Tamarix]]'' that are vigorously invasive.<ref name=fs-fed-tamaph/>

== History ==
Most botanists and Bible scholars believe that the ''eshel'' tree planted by [[Abraham]] in the [[Book of Genesis]], was ''Tamarix aphylla'',<ref name=Abraham-blog-2011-03-24/> [[Carl Linnaeus]] wrote that its name was derived from the [[Ancient Greek]]'' 'a'<nowiki/>'' "without", and'' 'phyllon''' "leaf".<ref name=Liddell-Scott-1980/>

In [[Urdu]] and [[Hindi]], the tree is called ''farash'' ({{lang|ur|فراش}}) and in [[Punjabi language|Punjabi]], it is called ''kooan'' ({{lang|pa|کواں}}). In [[Balochi language|Baluchi]], it is called ''shakargaaz'' or ''siahgaaz''. In [[Saraiki language|Saraiki]], it is called Khagal.<ref name=Aus-CIA-MN-050-13/> while in Pashto it is called Ghaz (غز).

== Chemistry ==
{{See also|galloyl|glucose}}
[[2,6-Digalloyl glucose]] and [[3,6-digalloyl glucose]] are [[gallotannin]]s which are found in the [[gall]]s of ''T. aphylla''.<ref name=Nawar-Hussein-1994/>
